Bernardino Ochino
ber-nar-dē'nō ō-kē'nō
n. (Bernardino Ochino, 1487–1564, vicar-general of the Capuchins who fled Rome for Geneva and ended his life in grave error)
Italian Bernardino, diminutive of Bernardo, bear-bold, from Germanic bern and hard; Ochino, a Sienese family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bernardino Ochino was the most celebrated preacher in Italy before he was the most notorious. Three times vicar-general of the Capuchins, he preached Lent at Naples in 1536 and at Venice to crowds that emptied the other churches, and there he fell in with Juan de Valdés and Peter Martyr Vermigli and learned the free justification of the sinner. Summoned to Rome by the new Inquisition in 1542, he crossed the Alps instead, pastored the Italian congregation at Geneva, served Augsburg, and under Edward VI held a prebend at Canterbury. Mary's accession drove him back to Zurich, and there in 1563 he printed his Dialogi XXX, which handled the doctrine of the Trinity loosely and in one dialogue allowed that a man might in some case take a second wife. Zurich deprived him; he died of plague in Moravia among the Anabaptists. The dictionary honours the man who gave up a cardinal's prospects for the reproach of Christ and names the end without softening it: a flight from error is not yet an arrival at the truth, and a gifted preacher who will not be bound by a confessing church drifts. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jo 2:19) is written of another case, but the warning stands over every unsettled man.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines apostasy as a total desertion of the faith one has professed, and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.

expand to see more

APOS'TASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.

HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.

PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who inculcates.

DRIFT, n. A driving; impulse; course of anything; tendency.

Key Scripture

1Jo 2:19 — "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us."

2Pe 2:1 — "But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction."

Heb 10:39 — "But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul."

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Modern Corruption

The great preacher who fled Rome and never arrived at a confession.

expand to see more

Ochino is regularly enlisted as an early hero of free inquiry, a man hounded by Geneva and Zurich as he had been by Rome, and the Dialogi are read as the first stirrings of liberty of conscience. The account will not stand. Zurich did not burn him and did not hunt him; a Reformed city removed a Reformed minister from a Reformed pulpit for printing what those churches confessed to be error about the Godhead and about marriage, which is discipline, not persecution. To call it persecution is to grant that a church owes its pulpit to any man who once suffered for the gospel.

The principle to recover is that courage does not sanctify doctrine. A man may be brave at Rome and wrong at Zurich, and the second does not cancel the first nor the first excuse the second. Paul fixes the measure where no reputation reaches it: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apostasia (G646), a falling away; hairesis (G139), a self-chosen faction or heresy.

expand to see more

Greek apostasia (G646) — a falling away, defection; 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

Greek hairesis (G139) — a choosing, a faction, a heresy; 2 Peter 2:1.

Greek pseudodidaskalos (G5572) — a false teacher; 2 Peter 2:1.

Greek hupostello (G5288) — to draw back, withdraw oneself; Hebrews 10:38.

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; Galatians 1:8.

Usage

"“They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jo 2:19) — the warning over every unsettled flight."

"“denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1) — where a loose doctrine of God ends."

"“But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition” (Heb 10:39) — the contrast the Italian martyrs made good."
